title: PyTone
description: Any image, rebuilt from glyphs. Terminal, HTML or SVG.

content.context: ASCII art is usually a novelty: a gray block of characters stuck in a terminal. PyTone treats it as a medium. It's a small Python CLI that rebuilds any image from glyphs and keeps each one's color, then writes the result as truecolor terminal output, a self-contained HTML page, or a scalable SVG you can drop into a README. The glyph ramp is an artistic choice, not a fixed setting. Saturn can be drawn in rings, the Moon in moon phases, and a Vermeer in circles that swell with the light. What began as a weekend extension of a tutorial grew into a hardened, well-tested tool, a gallery of thirty pieces, and a stage-by-stage guide to the pipeline drawn from its own output.
goals: Turn any image into text art with one command and no setup, via uvx
Output plain text, ANSI truecolor, HTML, or SVG from one shared pipeline
Make the glyph ramp, gradient, and density the creative controls
Explain each stage of the pipeline with diagrams built from its real output
Harden the tool for scripts and agents: atomic writes, source protection, clear exit codes
Prove the range with a gallery of old masters, space imagery, and iconic photography

artifacts.alt: PyTone: a snake made of halftone dots crossing a dot screen, above the PyTone wordmark
artifacts.label: Project Identity
artifacts.description: The logo is made with the tool itself. A snake drawn in halftone dots crosses a dot screen above a Space Grotesk wordmark, rendered in the circles ramp · ∘ ○ ◯ ● with a gradient in the Python logo's blue and gold.

artifacts.alt: The PyTone pipeline in six stages: image, resize, grayscale, glyph ramp, color and output, each showing its real result on a photo of Jupiter with the flags that control it
artifacts.label: From Picture to Glyphs
artifacts.description: Six small stages, each with one job and its own flags. Every picture in the diagram is the real output of that stage on a photo of Jupiter, and one command runs them all.

artifacts.code:
# Try it without installing
uvx --from git+https://github.com/interfaceconjurer/ascii-image-generator pytone photo.jpg

# One command, every stage
pytone jupiter.jpg -w 110 -c " ·∘○◯●" --gradient "#3D1A4D,#FFD700" -m svg -o jupiter.svg
artifacts.label: One Command
artifacts.description: No install needed to try it. The full command maps onto the stages: the source image, -w for the resize, -c for the ramp, --gradient for color, and -m and -o for the output.

artifacts.alt: Step 4, Glyph ramp: a brightness histogram split into one bucket per glyph, and the same picture drawn in classic, circle, block and star ramps
artifacts.label: The Ramp Is the Brush Stroke
artifacts.description: Each brightness falls into one bucket per character, ordered dark to light. The same grid drawn in four ramps shows that only the characters change, and with them the texture.

artifacts.alt: Step 5, Color: glyphs keep their source color, or take a diagonal gradient or a horizontal rainbow, then saturation and brightness multipliers
artifacts.label: Color That Keeps the Shape
artifacts.description: Glyphs keep their source color or take a gradient or rainbow. Both are modulated by brightness, so the subject still reads.

artifacts.alt: Step 6, Output: the same glyph grid as plain text, ANSI, HTML and SVG, with the trade-offs and file size of each
artifacts.label: Four Outputs
artifacts.description: The same glyph grid written as plain text, ANSI, HTML or SVG, with the strengths, trade-offs and real file size of each.

artifacts.label: Choosing an Output

content.whatsNext: Next is source prep. Many gallery pieces depend on ImageMagick levels, gamma and contrast applied before conversion, and folding those into PyTone would make the README commands fully reproducible. After that, wide-glyph and emoji alignment needs to work consistently across terminals.
